concept.body: A precise definition is a perfect sorting machine: every object is definitely IN or definitely OUT, no judgment calls. "All points at distance r from O" sorts every point of the plane; "a round shape" sorts almost nothing.

explanationVariants: "Coplanar lines that do not intersect" gives a yes/no test every pair of lines can take — that's what precise means.
Vague words like "slanted the same way" fail the sorting test: two people could disagree about the same pair of lines.

widget.prompt: Which is the PRECISE definition of parallel lines?

options.label: coplanar lines that do not intersect
options.feedback: Two clear tests — same plane? never meet? — and every pair of lines passes or fails definitively.

options.label: lines that slant the same way
options.feedback: "Slant the same way" isn't a test anyone can apply exactly — precise definitions leave no judgment calls.

options.label: lines that never touch
options.feedback: In 3-D, skew lines never touch either but aren't parallel — the definition must demand COPLANAR.

options.label: lines that stay pretty close together
options.feedback: "Pretty close" sorts nothing — a precise definition must decide every case cleanly.

steps.body: Three hats, three objects: a two-way arrow over AB means the **line**, a one-way arrow the **ray**, a plain bar the **segment**. NO hat — plain AB — means a **number**: the segment's length. So segments are **congruent** (≅, same size and shape) while lengths are **equal** (=, same number). Write segment AB ≅ segment CD, but AB = CD.

widget.prompt: Sort each statement: does it compare NUMBERS (=) or FIGURES (≅)?

items.label: the lengths of two boards are the same
items.feedback: A length is a number of centimeters — numbers compare with =.

items.label: two segments match exactly, end to end
items.feedback: "Match end to end" compares the segments themselves — figures are congruent (≅), not equal.

items.label: two angles have the same degree measure
items.feedback: A degree measure like 40° is a number, so the measures are EQUAL: m∠A = m∠B.

items.label: two angles are copies of each other
items.feedback: The angles themselves — the figures — are congruent: ∠A ≅ ∠B.

widget.missFeedback: Ask what is being compared: a measurement (number) takes =, the shape itself takes ≅.
widget.successFeedback: Numbers get =, figures get ≅ — and m∠A turns an angle into a number.

explanationVariants: AB with no hat is a length (a number), so AB = CD is the legal pairing; the segments themselves take ≅.
Match symbol to object type: = joins two numbers, ≅ joins two figures. Mixing them is a type error, like comparing 7 ≅ 7.

widget.prompt: Segments AB and CD match exactly. Which statement is written correctly?

options.label: AB = CD (comparing the lengths)
options.feedback: Plain AB and CD are numbers — the lengths — and numbers compare with =.

options.label: AB ≅ CD (comparing the lengths)
options.feedback: Plain AB is already a number, and numbers take =. The ≅ symbol is reserved for the figures themselves.

options.label: m(segment AB) ≅ m(segment CD)
options.feedback: Measures are numbers, and numbers take = — the m(...) wrapper makes ≅ doubly out of place.

options.label: AB = segment CD
options.feedback: This equates a number with a figure — a type mismatch no matter which symbol sits between them.

steps.body: The same discipline covers angles: **∠A is a figure; m∠A is a number** (its measure in degrees). ∠A ≅ ∠B and m∠A = m∠B say the same thing in two registers — and swapping their symbols is the classic notation error graders hunt for.

widget.prompt: A student writes: “m∠P ≅ m∠Q”. Which correction makes it right?

options.label: m∠P = m∠Q
options.feedback: The m turns each angle into a number, and numbers compare with =.

options.label: ∠P = ∠Q
options.feedback: Now it's figures joined by = — the error just moved. Figures take ≅.

options.label: m∠P ≅ ∠Q
options.feedback: This compares a number to a figure — a mismatch worse than the original.

options.label: Leave it — it's already correct
options.feedback: The m-values are numbers, and ≅ is the figure symbol; one of the two must change.

explanationVariants: ∠A is the figure; m∠A is its measure, a number of degrees. Only the m-version can equal 40.
You can't set a corner equal to a number — first take its measure. m∠A = 40° is the number-to-number statement.

widget.prompt: An angle at vertex A measures 40 degrees. Which statement records that correctly?

options.label: m∠A = 40°
options.feedback: m∠A is a number and 40° is a number — a legal = pairing.

options.label: ∠A = 40°
options.feedback: ∠A is the figure itself — a figure can't equal a number. The measure m∠A is what equals 40°.

options.label: ∠A ≅ 40°
options.feedback: ≅ joins two FIGURES, and 40° is a number — this mixes types in a new way.

options.label: m∠A ≅ 40°
options.feedback: Both sides are numbers here, so the symbol must be =, not the figure-symbol ≅.

steps.body: Where things meet: two distinct lines intersect in at most one **point**; a line meets a plane it doesn't lie in at exactly one point; two distinct planes intersect in a **line** (think of two walls meeting along their shared edge). The intersection is always a lower-rung object.

widget.prompt: Two distinct planes intersect (like two walls of a room). Their intersection is…

options.label: a line
options.feedback: The walls share their whole vertical crease — a straight path running forever with both planes: a line.

options.label: a point
options.feedback: A single point is what two LINES can share. Planes are too big to touch at just one point — the shared set runs on.

options.label: a segment
options.feedback: The crease doesn't stop where the room does — planes extend forever, so their shared set does too: a full line.

options.label: a plane
options.feedback: Sharing a whole plane would make them the SAME plane — but these are distinct.

hints: Check each line for a type match: numbers with =, figures with ≅.
XY with no hat is a number; ∠D without an m is a figure.
Only one line pairs its symbol with the right TYPE on both sides.
explanationVariants: Line by line: XY = 7 pairs number with number ✓. The others join a figure with = or a number with ≅ — type errors.
The test is one question, asked twice per statement: is each side a number or a figure? Both numbers → =; both figures → ≅; anything else is illegal.

widget.prompt: Which notebook line is correctly written?

options.label: XY = 7
options.feedback: XY without a hat is the LENGTH — a number — and 7 is a number. Numbers pair with =.

options.label: ∠D = ∠E
options.feedback: ∠D and ∠E are figures — they'd need ≅. (Their MEASURES, m∠D and m∠E, are what take =.)

options.label: m∠D ≅ 40°
options.feedback: m∠D and 40° are both numbers — the pairing must be m∠D = 40°.

options.label: segment XY ≅ 7
options.feedback: A segment is a figure and 7 is a number — no symbol can legally join those two types.

takeaways: Hats pick the object: line, ray, or segment; no hat = the length, a number.
Numbers take =; figures take ≅ — and m∠A is the number, ∠A the figure.
Intersections drop a rung: planes share a line, lines share at most a point.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: put numbers on segments and angles — and let B-between-A-and-C do arithmetic.
